Part 1

Precipitation in time and space

Why precipitation must be described at the right time and space scale

Precipitation varies in time and space

Key idea

Every precipitation question has a time scale and a space scale. Pick data that match both.

Time: temporal variation

Instantaneous, hourly, daily, monthly, seasonal, annual, interannual, decadal

Space: spatial variation

Points, plots, localities, regions, continents and oceans

Read the figure

Processes are placed by their spatial scale (vertical) and temporal scale (horizontal): from turbulence and tornadoes (seconds, under 1 km) to ENSO and climate variation (years to centuries, global).

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q1 Give one precipitation-related process that is short and local, and one that is long and global.

Short and local: turbulence, a tornado, a thunderstorm. Long and global: ENSO, climate variation, monsoon or trade wind patterns.

Q2 Why would monthly precipitation totals be the wrong data for designing an urban storm drain?

Urban drainage responds in minutes to hours, so the design needs short-duration rainfall intensity, not monthly totals that hide individual storms.

Part 2

Variation over time

Hyetographs, long-term records, filling missing data, and precipitation datasets

Hyetographs and rainfall intensity

Key idea

Intensity = depth ÷ duration. A hyetograph shows how rainfall intensity changes through a storm.

Read the two panels

  • (a) Hyetograph: rainfall intensity (in/h) in each 10-minute interval
  • (b) Cumulative curve: total depth accumulated over time

Connect them

Between 20 and 30 min the intensity is 3.5 in/h. Over 10 minutes (1/6 h) that adds 3.5 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.58 in, which is why curve (b) jumps from 0.43 to 1.02 in.

The steepest part of (b) is the most intense part of the storm.

Long-term temporal variability

Key idea

Long records show both year-to-year variation and a regular seasonal cycle.

Annual record (left)

Annual rainfall at Arba Minch, 1986–2005. Dots are individual years; the red line is the long-term average. Single years can sit far above or below it.

Seasonal cycle (right)

Monthly precipitation (bars) and temperature (line). Here precipitation falls mostly in winter, while temperature peaks in summer.

Filling missing data: the regression method

Key idea

Estimate missing values at one gauge from a strongly correlated nearby gauge.

Use it only when

  • Relatively few values are missing
  • The known data are highly representative
  • The missing data have a high correlation to the known data

Read the figure

  • Left: a daily record with a few missing days (red points)
  • Right: values at the target gauge plotted against a nearby gauge. The fitted line predicts the missing values

PRISM climate dataset

Key idea

PRISM provides gridded historical climate data at 800 m or 4 km resolution. It is very useful for research.

How PRISM works

“PRISM calculates a climate–elevation regression for each DEM grid cell, and stations entering the regression are assigned weights based primarily on the physiographic similarity of the station to the grid cell.”

Factors considered

Location, elevation, coastal proximity, topographic facet orientation, vertical atmospheric layer, topographic position and orographic effectiveness of the terrain.

Nearly 13,000 stations for precipitation and 10,000 for temperature.

City of Portland HYDRA rainfall network

Key idea

Precipitation data usually come by water year (October 1 – September 30), not by calendar year.

The HYDRA network is a set of rain gauges across the Portland area. Click a gauge on the map to see its record.

Water year

  • The 12-month period from October 1 to September 30 of the following year
  • Named for the calendar year in which it ends, which contains 9 of its 12 months
  • So the water year ending September 30, 2018 is water year 2018

Why October?

It starts the year at the beginning of the wet season, so one winter's storms fall in a single water year.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q3 A storm drops 0.6 in of rain in 15 minutes. What is its intensity in in/h?

Intensity = depth ÷ duration = 0.6 in ÷ 0.25 h = 2.4 in/h.

Q4 Which water year does December 15, 2026 belong to?

Water year 2027 (October 1, 2026 – September 30, 2027).

Q5 When is it appropriate to fill missing precipitation data by regression?

When only a few values are missing, the known data are representative, and the target gauge is highly correlated with the nearby gauge.

Part 3

Variation over space

Four methods for turning gauge readings into an average depth over a watershed

Spatial precipitation variability

Key idea

Not all land receives the same amount of precipitation, even within one state or one storm.

Read the maps

  • Left: long-term average annual precipitation. The coast and Cascades are wet (blue-green); eastern Oregon is dry (red)
  • Right: a single storm on radar, falling on only part of the region

Why it matters

A watershed budget needs one number for precipitation over the whole area, but gauges only measure points. The rest of this part covers how to bridge that gap.

Effective uniform depth (EUD)

Key idea

For a water budget we need the effective uniform depth: the single depth that, spread evenly over the basin, gives the same total.

  • If the rain-gauge network has uniform density, a simple arithmetic average of the gauge data is enough
  • If the network is not uniform, the gauges must be weighted

Read the figure

A basin outline with gauge readings (in inches). Some gauges sit outside the boundary and the network is uneven. We will reuse this basin for the Thiessen method.

Arithmetic mean method

  1. Arithmetic mean
  2. Isohyetal
  3. Thiessen polygons
  4. Inverse distance (IDW)
Key idea

The simplest way to get areal average precipitation: average the gauge readings.

P̄ = (1/N) Σ Pᵢ

Two requirements

1. Gauges must be uniformly distributed

2. Gauge readings should not vary greatly from the mean

Worked example

P₁ = 10 mm, P₂ = 20 mm, P₃ = 30 mm

P̄ = (10 + 20 + 30) / 3 = 20 mm

Read the figure

Five stations inside a river basin: (0.55 + 0.87 + 2.33 + 5.40 + 1.89) / 5 = 2.21 in.

Isohyetal method

  1. Arithmetic mean
  2. Isohyetal
  3. Thiessen polygons
  4. Inverse distance (IDW)
Key idea

Draw isohyets, lines of equal rainfall like elevation contours, then weight each band by its area.

Steps

1. Construct isohyets (rainfall contour lines)

2. Compute the area between each pair of adjacent isohyets

3. Compute the average precipitation for each band

4. Compute the areal average:

P̄ = (1/A) Σ Aᵢ Pᵢ

Worked example (figure, A = 47)

P̄ = (5×5 + 18×15 + 12×25 + 12×35) / 47 = 1,015 / 47 = 21.6 mm

Thiessen polygon method: building the polygons

  1. Arithmetic mean
  2. Isohyetal
  3. Thiessen polygons
  4. Inverse distance (IDW)
Key idea

Each gauge represents the part of the basin closest to it. Its weight is the area of that part.

To determine the areas

1. Join adjacent gauges with lines

2. Draw a perpendicular bisector at the midpoint of each line

3. Extend the bisectors to form polygons around each station

4. Measure each polygon's area to get the area-weighted average

The assumption

Any point in the watershed receives the same rainfall as the nearest gauge. A gauge's reading applies halfway to the next station in any direction.

Thiessen polygon method: worked example

  1. Arithmetic mean
  2. Isohyetal
  3. Thiessen polygons
  4. Inverse distance (IDW)
Key idea

Thiessen uses the same formula as the isohyetal method, but the areas come from polygons around gauges.

P̄ = (1/A) Σ Aᵢ Pᵢ

Worked example

  • P₁ = 10 mm, A₁ = 12 km²
  • P₂ = 20 mm, A₂ = 15 km²
  • P₃ = 30 mm, A₃ = 20 km²
  • Total area A = 47 km²

P̄ = (12×10 + 15×20 + 20×30) / 47 = 1,020 / 47 = 21.7 mm

Gauge 3 covers the largest area, so it pulls the average above the simple mean of 20 mm.

Inverse distance weighting (IDW)

  1. Arithmetic mean
  2. Isohyetal
  3. Thiessen polygons
  4. Inverse distance (IDW)
Key idea

A prediction at an ungauged point is influenced more by nearby gauges than distant ones: weight = 1 / d².

Steps

1. Compute the distance dᵢ from the ungauged point to each gauge: d = √((x₁ − x₂)² + (y₁ − y₂)²)

2. Compute the weighted estimate:

P̂ = Σ(Pᵢ / dᵢ²) / Σ(1 / dᵢ²)

Worked example (figure)

P₁ = 10 at d = 25; P₂ = 20 at d = 15; P₃ = 30 at d = 10

P̂ = (10/25² + 20/15² + 30/10²) / (1/25² + 1/15² + 1/10²) = 25.24 mm

The closest gauge (30 mm) dominates the estimate.

When to use which method?

Key idea

Match the method to the gauge network and the terrain.

Arithmetic average

Gauges evenly distributed. Good for level terrain.

Isohyetal (contour) area-weighted average

Draw lines of equal rainfall, like a contour map. Good for mountainous areas.

Thiessen polygons: area-weighted average

Area closest to each gauge. Good for non-uniform gauge distribution; not good for mountains.

Inverse distance weighting (IDW)

Accounts for spatial autocorrelation (Tobler's First Law of Geography). Useful with limited stations and complex topography.

Tobler's First Law

“Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.” This is the idea behind IDW.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q6 Three gauges read 12, 18 and 30 mm. What is the arithmetic mean? When would this be a poor estimate?

(12 + 18 + 30) / 3 = 20 mm. It is poor if the gauges are unevenly distributed or readings vary greatly, such as in mountainous terrain.

Q7 Thiessen polygons give gauge A (10 mm) 30 km² and gauge B (40 mm) 10 km². What is the areal average?

P̄ = (30×10 + 10×40) / 40 = 700 / 40 = 17.5 mm.

Q8 Using IDW, an ungauged point is 10 km from gauge A (10 mm) and 20 km from gauge B (40 mm). Estimate its precipitation.

Weights: 1/100 = 0.01 and 1/400 = 0.0025. P̂ = (10×0.01 + 40×0.0025) / 0.0125 = 0.2 / 0.0125 = 16 mm.

Q9 Which method would you choose for a mountainous watershed with a dense gauge network, and why?

The isohyetal method: contours of equal rainfall can follow the strong orographic gradients that Thiessen polygons ignore.

Part 4

Measuring precipitation

Precipitation depth, rain gauges, and radar and satellite observation

Precipitation is measured as a depth

Key idea

Rain and snow are both measured as a depth, in millimeters or inches: the layer of liquid water that would cover the area.

One millimeter of precipitation is the quantity needed to cover the area with a 1 mm layer of liquid water.

So how much water is “1 inch”?

It depends on the area you care about. Volume = depth × area.

Example: 1 inch (0.0254 m) over 1 km² (1,000,000 m²) = 25,400 m³ of water.

Read the map

Thousands of volunteer stations across the U.S. report daily precipitation.

Standard rain gauge

Key idea

A rain gauge collects the water falling on it and records the change in depth over time.

Read the figures

  • Left: a standard gauge. The funnel concentrates rain into a narrow inner tube, so small depths can be read precisely. Here 2.25 inches have fallen
  • Middle: a simple plastic gauge on a post
  • Right: a homemade gauge from a plastic bottle

Depth is usually expressed in millimeters or inches.

Tipping bucket gauge

Key idea

A tipping bucket records rainfall electronically by counting how many times a small bucket of known volume fills and tips.

How it works

1. Rain fills one side of a small bucket to a limit set by the manufacturer or operator

2. When full, the bucket tips and hits a calibration/stop screw

3. The other bucket is lifted into place and starts to fill

4. Each tip is counted; the process repeats as long as it rains

Read the photo

The ring of slats around the gauge is a wind shield, which reduces undercatch in windy conditions.

Weighing recording gauge

Key idea

A weighing gauge measures the weight of collected water over time and converts it to rainfall depth.

How it works

Precipitation falls through the funnel into a collecting bucket. A mechanical (spring) balance senses the weight, and a pen records it on a rotating chart.

Advantage

Because it weighs rather than measures volume, it also records snow and other solid precipitation.

Read the photo

The gauge sits inside an Alter-type wind shield of hanging slats.

Radar and satellite

Key idea

Radar and satellites measure precipitation over large areas and are essential for forecasting extreme weather.

  • We depend on them heavily to forecast events like hurricanes and atmospheric rivers
  • Spaceborne radar can observe the three-dimensional structure of precipitation
  • Satellite observations can distinguish rain, snow and other types, and show storm structure, intensity and dynamics

Read the images

Top: a NEXRAD radar dome and a radar reflectivity map of the Pacific Northwest. Bottom: an atmospheric river reaching the West Coast, and a hurricane on radar.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q10 How many cubic meters of water fall when 10 mm of rain covers a 5 km² watershed?

0.01 m × 5,000,000 m² = 50,000 m³.

Q11 What does a tipping bucket gauge actually count, and how is that turned into depth?

It counts the number of tips; each tip is a known volume (a fixed depth over the collector area), so depth = tips × depth per tip.

Q12 Name one advantage of a weighing gauge and one advantage of radar over a standard rain gauge.

Weighing gauge: records continuously and handles snow. Radar: covers large areas and shows storm structure, useful for forecasting.
